course.title: Environmental Science
course.description: How living things, energy, and matter connect across the planet — from food webs and nutrient cycles to climate, resources, and the human footprint. Structure adapted from CK-12 Earth Science (CC BY-NC 3.0).

questions.prompt: An ecosystem is best defined as…
options: only the animals in an area
a community of living things interacting with their physical environment
a group of the same species
questions.explanation: An ecosystem combines the biotic community and the abiotic environment — see 'Ecosystems and energy flow'.

questions.prompt: The ultimate source of energy for most ecosystems is…
questions.explanation: Producers capture sunlight through photosynthesis — see 'Ecosystems and energy flow'.

questions.prompt: The process by which plants remove carbon dioxide from the air is…
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis fixes atmospheric CO2 into sugars — see 'Biogeochemical cycles'.

questions.prompt: Biodiversity refers to…
options: the total number of animals only
the variety of life at genetic, species, and ecosystem levels
the biggest species in a habitat
questions.explanation: Biodiversity spans genes, species, and ecosystems — see 'Biodiversity'.

questions.prompt: The greenhouse effect works because certain gases…
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared energy — see 'Climate and the greenhouse effect'.

questions.prompt: A renewable resource is one that…
options: is replenished naturally on a human timescale
questions.explanation: Renewables like sunlight and wind refill faster than we use them.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of a point-source pollutant?
options: a factory discharge pipe into a river
questions.explanation: Point sources come from a single identifiable location.

questions.prompt: Conservation is best described as…
options: the careful management and protection of natural resources
letting nature take its course with no management
questions.explanation: Conservation balances use and protection — see 'Human impact and conservation'.

lessons.title: Ecosystems and energy flow
lessons.grammar_note: Energy flows one way; matter cycles. Keep that contrast handy all course.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Trace energy from the Sun through a food chain and explain why food chains are short. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, where does the energy in almost every ecosystem originally come from?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: An *ecosystem* is a community of organisms plus the non-living environment they interact with. *Producers* (mostly plants and algae) capture sunlight and build sugars by photosynthesis. *Consumers* eat producers or other consumers, and *decomposers* break down dead matter. Energy moves along a *food chain* from one *trophic level* to the next, but only about 10% of the energy stored at one level is passed to the next — the rest is lost as heat during respiration. That '10% rule' is why food chains rarely have more than four or five links.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Follow the energy: grass captures 10,000 units of solar energy. A grasshopper eating the grass retains roughly 1,000 units; a shrew eating grasshoppers keeps about 100; a hawk eating shrews gets around 10. Ninety percent is lost at each step, so top predators need a very large base of producers to survive.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Classify each organism as producer, consumer, or decomposer: (1) an oak tree, (2) a fungus on a rotting log, (3) a deer, (4) a hawk, (5) pond algae. Answers: (1) producer, (2) decomposer, (3) consumer, (4) consumer, (5) producer.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking energy 'cycles' like water — energy flows one way and is lost as heat, so ecosystems need a constant solar input. Mistake: assuming all the energy passes up the chain. Exit: (a) About what fraction of energy transfers between trophic levels? (b) What do decomposers return to the soil? Answers: about 10%; nutrients (matter).

lessons.title: Biogeochemical cycles: carbon, water, and nitrogen
lessons.grammar_note: A 'reservoir' is where matter is stored; a 'flux' is a movement between reservoirs.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe how carbon, water, and nitrogen move between living things, air, water, and rock. Warm-up: which process pulls carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Unlike energy, matter is recycled through *biogeochemical cycles*. In the *carbon cycle*, photosynthesis moves carbon from the air into living tissue, while respiration, decomposition, and combustion return it to the atmosphere as CO2. In the *water cycle*, energy from the Sun drives evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and runoff. In the *nitrogen cycle*, nitrogen gas (N2) makes up most of the air but must be *fixed* by bacteria (or lightning) into ammonia and nitrates before plants can use it; *denitrifying* bacteria eventually return N2 to the air. Each cycle stores matter in *reservoirs* (oceans, rock, atmosphere, living things) and moves it between them.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Trace one carbon atom: it starts as CO2 in the air, is fixed into glucose by a corn plant (photosynthesis), is eaten by a cow (now part of tissue), is exhaled by the cow as CO2 (respiration) — or, if the cow's remains are buried for millions of years, becomes fossil fuel until burning (combustion) releases it again.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Name the process for each move: (1) liquid water in a lake becomes vapor, (2) plants convert CO2 into sugar, (3) soil bacteria turn N2 into usable nitrogen compounds, (4) an animal breathes out CO2. Answers: (1) evaporation, (2) photosynthesis, (3) nitrogen fixation, (4) respiration.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking plants can use the nitrogen gas they are surrounded by — they cannot, until bacteria fix it. Mistake: forgetting the ocean is a huge carbon reservoir. Exit: (a) Which organisms make atmospheric nitrogen usable? (b) Name two processes that return CO2 to the air. Answers: nitrogen-fixing bacteria; respiration, decomposition, and combustion (any two).

lessons.title: Biodiversity and why it matters
lessons.grammar_note: Three levels of biodiversity: genetic, species, ecosystem.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define biodiversity at three levels and explain why variety makes ecosystems more stable. Warm-up: is biodiversity only about counting the number of species?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Biodiversity* is the variety of life, measured at three levels: *genetic diversity* (variation within a species), *species diversity* (the number and abundance of different species), and *ecosystem diversity* (the range of habitats in a region). Diversity provides *ecosystem services* — pollination, clean water, fertile soil, and climate regulation — and acts like insurance: if one species is lost, others may fill its role. A *keystone species* has an effect out of proportion to its numbers; remove it and the whole community can shift. Biodiversity is threatened by habitat loss, invasive species, pollution, overharvesting, and climate change.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Sea otters are a keystone species. Otters eat sea urchins; urchins eat kelp. Where otters were hunted out, urchin populations exploded and grazed kelp forests down to bare rock, wiping out the many species that depended on the kelp. Protecting one predator preserved an entire ecosystem.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Identify the level of biodiversity: (1) different alleles for coat color in a wolf pack, (2) the number of bird species in a forest, (3) a landscape with wetlands, grasslands, and woodlands. Then: (4) name one threat to biodiversity. Answers: (1) genetic, (2) species, (3) ecosystem, (4) habitat loss (or invasive species, pollution, overharvesting, climate change).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: equating biodiversity with just a species count — genetic and ecosystem variety matter too. Mistake: thinking a rare species can't be important — keystone species are often not the most numerous. Exit: (a) Name the three levels of biodiversity. (b) What is a keystone species? Answers: genetic, species, ecosystem; a species whose impact on its community is far larger than its abundance suggests.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much energy passes from one trophic level to the next?
questions.explanation: The 10% rule — most energy is lost as heat.

questions.prompt: Which statement is correct?
options: Energy cycles but matter flows one way
Matter cycles but energy flows one way
questions.explanation: Matter is recycled; energy flows one way and is lost as heat.

questions.prompt: Plants cannot use atmospheric nitrogen gas until it is…
options: fixed by bacteria into usable compounds
questions.explanation: Nitrogen fixation makes N2 available to plants.

questions.prompt: Which process removes CO2 from the atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis fixes atmospheric carbon into sugars.

questions.prompt: A keystone species is one that…
options: has an impact far greater than its abundance
questions.explanation: Its influence is out of proportion to its numbers.

questions.prompt: Decomposers are important because they…
questions.explanation: They recycle matter back into the ecosystem.

lessons.title: Climate and the greenhouse effect
lessons.grammar_note: Weather is short-term; climate is the long-term average.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain the natural greenhouse effect and how adding greenhouse gases warms the planet. Warm-up: what is the difference between weather and climate?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Weather* is the day-to-day state of the atmosphere; *climate* is the long-term average over decades. Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms Earth's surface, which radiates energy back as *infrared* (heat). *Greenhouse gases* — carbon dioxide, methane, water vapor — absorb some of that outgoing heat and re-radiate it, keeping the surface about 33°C warmer than it would otherwise be. This natural greenhouse effect makes Earth livable. Burning fossil fuels and clearing forests add extra CO2 and methane, thickening the 'blanket' and driving *global warming* and broader *climate change*: rising average temperatures, melting ice, higher seas, and shifting weather patterns.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Think of a parked car in the Sun. Sunlight enters through the glass and warms the seats; the warm interior radiates infrared, but the glass traps much of it, so the car grows far hotter than the air outside. Greenhouse gases act like that glass for the whole planet — letting sunlight in but slowing heat's escape.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Label each as weather or climate: (1) 'It rained here yesterday', (2) 'This desert averages 2 cm of rain a year', (3) 'A blizzard is forecast tomorrow', (4) 'Summers here have warmed 1.5°C since 1900'. Then: (5) name one greenhouse gas. Answers: (1) weather, (2) climate, (3) weather, (4) climate, (5) carbon dioxide (or methane, water vapor).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing the greenhouse effect with the ozone hole — they are separate problems. Mistake: pointing to one cold day to dispute climate change (that's weather, not climate). Exit: (a) What kind of radiation do greenhouse gases trap? (b) Is a single hot afternoon weather or climate? Answers: infrared (heat); weather.

lessons.title: Human impact and conservation
lessons.grammar_note: Sustainability means meeting today's needs without robbing the future.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe major human impacts on the environment and the strategies used to reduce them. Warm-up: what does it mean to use a resource 'sustainably'?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Human activity reshapes ecosystems through *habitat destruction* (deforestation, urban sprawl), *pollution* (releasing harmful substances into air, water, and soil), *overharvesting* (overfishing, overhunting), and *climate change*. *Conservation* is the careful management and protection of natural resources so they last. Strategies include protected areas and national parks, restoring damaged habitats, laws that limit pollution and harvesting, switching to *renewable resources* like solar and wind, and the everyday practice of *reduce, reuse, recycle*. *Sustainability* — meeting present needs without compromising future generations — is the guiding goal.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: The story of the ozone layer shows conservation working. Scientists linked CFC chemicals to the thinning of stratospheric ozone. Nations agreed under the Montreal Protocol to phase out CFCs, and the ozone layer has since begun to recover — evidence that identifying a cause and changing behavior can reverse environmental damage.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Match each impact to a conservation response: impacts — (1) overfishing, (2) deforestation, (3) fossil-fuel emissions; responses — (a) reforestation, (b) catch limits, (c) shift to solar and wind. Then: (4) give one example of 'reduce, reuse, recycle'. Answers: 1-b, 2-a, 3-c; (4) e.g. reusing a water bottle instead of buying single-use plastic.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking conservation means never using resources — it means using them wisely so they persist. Mistake: assuming individual action doesn't matter; small choices scale across billions of people. Exit: (a) Define sustainability in your own words. (b) Name one renewable energy source. Answers: meeting present needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs; solar (or wind, hydro, geothermal).

questions.prompt: Climate is best described as…
questions.explanation: Climate is weather averaged over decades.

questions.prompt: Greenhouse gases warm the planet by…
options: absorbing and re-emitting outgoing infrared heat
questions.explanation: They trap heat radiated by Earth's surface.

questions.prompt: Which pair are both renewable resources?
questions.explanation: Sunlight and wind are replenished naturally.

questions.prompt: Sustainability means…
options: meeting present needs without harming future generations
using resources as fast as possible
questions.explanation: It balances present use with future needs.

questions.prompt: The recovery of the ozone layer after the Montreal Protocol shows that…
options: coordinated action can undo environmental damage
questions.explanation: Phasing out CFCs let the ozone layer recover.

questions.prompt: Which human activity most directly reduces biodiversity?
questions.explanation: Destroying habitat removes the places species need to live.

lessons.title: Applied project: audit a local ecosystem

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Choose a real place you can picture — a park, pond, garden, vacant lot, or stretch of coast. You will describe it as an ecosystem and propose one conservation action. You are planning and reasoning, not running a full field study.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) Name at least one producer, one consumer, and one decomposer in your chosen place. 2) Trace a short food chain and note where the Sun's energy enters. 3) Identify one human impact affecting the site (pollution, habitat loss, invasive species, or climate change). 4) Propose one realistic conservation or sustainability action and explain how it would help.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ You correctly identified a producer, consumer, and decomposer. ✔ Your food chain shows energy entering from the Sun and flowing one direction. ✔ The human impact you named genuinely applies to the site. ✔ Your proposed action clearly addresses that impact and moves toward sustainability. If all four are true, you've analyzed a place the way an environmental scientist would.
